books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Presidential election results, November 4, 1856. Figures from the American Presidency Project (presidency.ucsb.edu/statistics/elections/1856); 296 electoral votes in all, 149 needed to win. Fillmore carried only Maryland.
stimulus.text:
| Candidate | Party | Popular votes | Share | Electoral votes |
| James Buchanan | Democratic | 1,836,072 | 45.3% | 174 |
| John C. Frémont | Republican | 1,342,345 | 33.1% | 114 |
| Millard Fillmore | American (Know-Nothing) | 873,053 | 21.5% | 8 |

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The table best supports the conclusion that the Republican Party in 1856

rationales.A: Background from the books: the party was born in 1854, yet by 1856 it ran second, with 114 electoral votes and a third of the popular vote.
rationales.B: Frémont won almost no votes in the slave states; the South voted for Buchanan and Fillmore.
rationales.C: Frémont’s 114 electoral votes all came from free states; he carried no slave state.
rationales.D: Frémont won 11 free states, including the largest ones; he did not lose them all.
rationales.general:
1. Note the party’s age: Background from the books: the Republicans were born in 1854, two years before this election.
2. Read its result: 114 electoral votes, 33.1 percent of the popular vote, second place.
3. See what it means: a sectional party had become the nation’s second party in a single leap.
Remember: a new party’s strength is measured by how fast it climbs, not by whether it wins at once.
